subsystems.name: Collector swarm
subsystems.role: captures starlight — not one solid shell, but billions of independent free-flying elements in orbit.

subsystems.name: Orbital architecture
subsystems.role: keeps the elements in stable orbits without colliding or drifting into the star.

subsystems.name: Materials and thermal control
subsystems.role: survives micrometeoroids, radiation and the heat load of concentrated sunlight.
parts: radiators sized to reject absorbed energy

subsystems.name: Manufacturing and replication
subsystems.role: builds the swarm from local material rather than launching it from a planet.

subsystems.name: Power transport and distribution
subsystems.role: moves energy from collectors to wherever it is used.

subsystems.name: Control network
subsystems.role: coordinates a structure too large for any human operator.

buildSteps.title: Choose the raw material
buildSteps.detail: The swarm's mass has to come from somewhere. Capturing even a fraction of a Sun-like star's output requires collector area on the order of 10^14 km² — hundreds of thousands of times Earth's surface. At a micrometre thickness that is roughly 10^21 kg of material, comparable to a small planet, so a rocky body or a large asteroid would be dismantled.

buildSteps.title: Mine and refine
buildSteps.detail: Robotic miners break up the body and feed smelters and vapour-deposition plants that turn rock and metal into structural film and photovoltaic layers.

buildSteps.title: Mass-produce collectors
buildSteps.detail: The decisive step is a factory that can copy itself. Only exponential replication — each unit building more units — can turn a small seed industry into enough hardware to matter on stellar scales.

buildSteps.title: Place elements into orbit
buildSteps.detail: Collectors are released onto carefully chosen orbits around the star, spaced to avoid shadowing each other and to keep station without a solid structure. Light-pressure sails or small thrusters hold position.

buildSteps.title: Extract and convert power
buildSteps.detail: Each element converts the starlight it intercepts to electricity or directs it by reflection; beamed microwave or laser links carry the energy inward to where it is used.

buildSteps.title: Manage heat
buildSteps.detail: Every watt captured must eventually be radiated away. In practice the swarm's waste heat would be re-radiated in the infrared, roughly at the temperature its radiators can sustain - a few hundred kelvin.

buildSteps.title: Expand by replication
buildSteps.detail: The factory fleet grows itself using more mined material, steadily raising the fraction of starlight intercepted. A solid rigid shell is not used: a shell around a star experiences essentially no net gravitational force at any point and would drift into it, so the swarm of independent orbiters is the physically sensible form.

buildSteps.title: Maintain and recycle
buildSteps.detail: Elements degrade under radiation and dust strikes and must be replaced from the same material stream, indefinitely.

prerequisites.why: nothing like an exponentially self-copying factory exists on Earth or in orbit, yet it is the only plausible route to stellar-scale hardware.
sample-return missions have brought back small amounts of asteroidal material, but mining and refining it in space is not demonstrated.
launch costs have fallen sharply, but a swarm cannot be launched from Earth at any plausible cost - it must be built in space.

prerequisites.tech: Large thin-film photovoltaics and deployable structures
prerequisites.why: thin-film solar and large lightweight space structures exist; nothing at the scale or durability a collector swarm needs.
microwave and laser power transmission has been demonstrated in experiments, not as an interplanetary energy grid.

prerequisites.tech: Orbital traffic coordination at extreme scale
prerequisites.why: managing billions of bodies in neighbouring orbits without collisions is an unsolved control problem.

pathway.milestone: robotic in-space assembly, asteroid sample return, and infrared sky surveys that look for the waste heat of any partial swarm already out there
pathway.unlocks: the engineering toolkit and the observational test.

pathway.milestone: small-scale in-space manufacturing from asteroidal or lunar material, plus kilometre-class beamed-power demonstrations
pathway.unlocks: the first hardware built off Earth from off-Earth material.

pathway.milestone: a free-flying 'seed' swarm of a few thousand coordinated collectors around a star
pathway.unlocks: proof that autonomous replication and orbital control work in practice.

pathway.milestone: self-replicating expansion to intercept a measurable fraction of a star's light
pathway.unlocks: a stellar-scale energy supply, and an unambiguous infrared signature visible to distant observers.

pathway.milestone: full capture of a star's output (a Kardashev Type II civilisation, in the 1964 classification)
pathway.unlocks: energy supply limited only by the star itself - if the materials, thermodynamics and control problems can all be solved.
